Maladaptive Strategies.value: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
make sure never to be alone with another person

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

issues.explanation: 'Dogs' as a primary trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of this military trauma profile: the other triggers/threat items center on interpersonal danger from men, being watched, and sudden human movements, with no supporting memory/appraisal content linking animals to the trauma. This makes the dog trigger clinically incoherent within the selected five components.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: 'Gambling' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The formulation strongly links Threat → Maladaptive Strategies and Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers, but the other selected strategies (overworking, never being alone with another person) plausibly manage interpersonal threat and hypervigilance, whereas gambling does not map clearly onto the endorsed trigger/threat pattern and reads as addressing a different problem domain.

vignette:
Priya was sixty-six, but the memory that ran her life was from a time when she was barely a woman. Forty years ago, in a makeshift clinic during the war, she had been a young midwife tending to the wounded. The soldiers came at dusk. They separated her from the others, taking her to a small, windowless room for questioning. The details had blurred into a suffocating feeling: the rough fabric of their uniforms, the claustrophobic presence of so many men in a tight space, and most of all, the weight of their eyes on her, watching her every breath as if it were a confession. She was eventually released, physically unharmed, but something inside her had been permanently calibrated to threat.

Forty years later, the soldiers were gone, but the feeling of being pinned by their gaze remained. Priya had built a distinguished career as a midwife in a busy American hospital, a place that should have felt safe. Yet, the building was a landscape of hidden mines. A security guard rounding the corner in his crisp uniform was enough to make her breath catch, her body instantly on guard. This immediate sense of threat would manifest as a physical inability to relax; her shoulders would hike up to her ears, and she would feel a frantic, superalert energy buzz under her skin, scanning for an escape that wasn't needed. The sudden movement of a patient's husband reaching for a glass of water could send a jolt of pure ice through her veins, her mind screaming danger before she could even process the harmlessness of the gesture.

Her response to this constant, simmering sense of danger was to build a fortress of activity and avoidance. She had come to believe that safety lay in perpetual motion and absolute control over her environment. She took on extra shifts, arriving early and staying late, throwing herself into charting and administrative tasks until her mind was too numb with exhaustion to feel afraid. This overworking was her primary anesthetic. More deliberately, she engineered her life to never be alone, especially not with men. At the hospital, she would ensure a student or a junior colleague was always with her during consultations. At home, she would wait for her husband to return before going into the basement. This constant vigilance for potentially dangerous people became a full-time job layered on top of her actual one, leaving her perpetually drained.

Over the decades, these strategies began to feed the very anxiety they were meant to quell. Her relentless overworking meant she spent more time than anyone else in the hospital, a place dense with her triggers. More shifts meant more encounters with uniformed security, more fathers-to-be in waiting rooms, more moments under the fluorescent lights where she felt exposed and observed. Her strategy of never being alone had, paradoxically, made the presence of a single man more menacing. By constantly scanning rooms and planning her movements to avoid being isolated with a male colleague or patient's family member, she was always rehearsing the danger, making it feel more imminent and real. Her hypervigilance for dangerous people meant she was always looking for them, and in doing so, she became intensely sensitive to the simple act of being perceived, interpreting a neutral glance as a predatory stare. The fortress had become a prison, its walls constricting year by year.

The breaking point came not with a dramatic event, but with a simple administrative change. A new hospital policy mandated that senior midwives conduct one-on-one prenatal counseling sessions to build patient rapport. There was no longer any justification for having a junior colleague in the room. The thought of sitting alone with a male patient, the door closed, felt like a reenactment she could not survive. After decades of successfully managing her world, her carefully constructed system had failed. Priya finally sought help, not because the memories were worse, but because her ways of outrunning them had led her to a dead end. She was exhausted, terrified of being seen as incompetent, and haunted by the quiet, desperate hope that she might one day be able to sit in a room and simply breathe.
